name: Red yeast rice

lead: Red yeast rice is rice fermented with Monascus mold, used for centuries in Chinese food and medicine and now sold for cholesterol. It appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the heart and body healthy over decades.

It contains monacolin K, identical to lovastatin, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that makes cholesterol. Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol, and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events. It has not been studied for appearance outcomes.

paras: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually as part of a cholesterol or longevity routine, often as an alternative some people consider alongside diet changes.

Reported effects resemble statins, including muscle and liver problems. Monacolin content varies and some products contain citrinin; EFSA in 2018 found no safe intake for monacolin preparations, and the FDA treats products with substantial monacolin K as drugs.

angle.text: Red yeast rice is taken for cholesterol and appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the body healthy over decades. Its cholesterol effect has been studied in trials; it is not used for a direct appearance outcome.

lead: Red yeast rice is rice fermented with the mold Monascus purpureus. It has long been used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine and is now sold as a supplement for cholesterol [1][2]. It contains monacolins, including monacolin K, which is chemically identical to the drug lovastatin [2][3].

Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol [4][5][6], and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events [7]. Safety concerns include variable monacolin content, possible citrinin contamination and statin-like muscle and liver effects [2][8]. It is included here as a longevity and cardiovascular supplement; no evidence on appearance outcomes was found.

paras: Wikipedia dates culinary use in China to at least the first century CE and describes the Ben Cao Gang Mu (c. 1590) recommending it for circulation and digestion [2]. In the late 1970s researchers in the United States and Japan isolated lovastatin and monacolins, and monacolin K was found to be identical to lovastatin [2][3].

A 12-week double-blind randomized trial in 83 US adults tested a proprietary Chinese red yeast rice supplement for cholesterol lowering [4]. A 2006 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined it for primary hyperlipidemia [5], and a 2015 meta-analysis reported significant LDL reduction while noting safety was uncertain [6]. A randomized trial in statin-intolerant patients was published in 2009 [9]. In the Chinese Coronary Secondary Prevention Study, nearly 5,000 patients with prior myocardial infarction took Xuezhikang [7]; Wikipedia reports reduced heart attacks and deaths [2].

Monacolin content varies widely between products and is rarely labeled, and some products contain citrinin, a kidney-toxic fungal compound [2]. Myopathy and liver injury have been reported, mirroring statin effects [2][10]. EFSA concluded in 2018 that no safe intake could be established for monacolin-containing preparations [2]. In 2024 Japanese authorities ordered recalls of Kobayashi Pharmaceutical products after reports of illness; the company found puberulic acid in recalled lots [2].

The FDA moved against the product Cholestin in 1998, with an appeals court ruling for the agency in 2001, and issued warning letters in 2007 [2]. Products containing monacolin K are regulated as drugs; many products contain negligible monacolins and make no cholesterol claims [2].

Randomized trials report LDL-lowering with red yeast rice [4][5][6][9] and reduced cardiovascular events in Chinese post-infarction patients [7]. No studies of red yeast rice for body fat, weight or appearance were found.
